opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a gap between the vision and what's actually going to work in practice. The vision is really appealing: instead of navigating a dozen different websites and apps, each with its own quirky interface, you just tell ChatGPT what you want, book me a flight, order groceries, find me a restaurant, and it handles everything behind the scenes. And technically you can see why people are excited, because language models are surprisingly good at taking a fuzzy request and turning it into a structured API call.

But I see a few difficulties. The first is reliability. When you're chatting with a model and it makes a mistake, it's usually low stakes, you notice and correct it. When it's acting on your behalf, buying something, sending an email, making a reservation, the cost of errors goes way up. Even a small failure rate compounds over multi-step tasks. If each step is right 95% of the time and you chain ten of them, you're failing a lot. And these failures often aren't obvious to the user, which is worse.

The second is security. Once the model reads content from the web and can also take actions, you open the door to prompt injection. A webpage, an email, or a product listing can contain text that effectively hijacks the assistant. We don't have a robust solution, and I'd be cautious about anyone who says we do. Connecting a model to your accounts and payment methods makes that a much more serious problem.

The third is economic and arguably the most underappreciated. Websites and apps aren't neutral pipes for information. Their business models depend on you visiting them, seeing their branding, ads, upsells, recommendations. If ChatGPT becomes the intermediary, a lot of companies lose that relationship with the customer, so they have strong incentives not to cooperate, or to cooperate only on their terms. We've seen versions of this before, think of how companies reacted to aggregators or screen scrapers. So the universal interface isn't just a technical question; it depends on a lot of businesses agreeing to become a back end for someone else's front end.

And finally, there's a user experience point. For many tasks, a graphical interface is actually better than conversation. If I'm choosing a hotel, I want to scan photos, maps, prices side by side. Typing back and forth with a chatbot can be slower and less transparent. So I think chat will become an important interface for certain tasks, but replacing all the interfaces we have is a much harder claim, and I'd expect progress to be slower and messier than the hype suggests.

r001.rationale: It says companies may have to “become a back end for someone else’s front end,” describing websites and apps as backend providers.

r002.rationale: It mentions API calls and backend services, but does not frame direct provider integration as an alternative to an agent navigating the web generally.

r003.rationale: It notes providers may resist cooperating, but does not connect that reluctance to limited uptake of GPT integrations.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are really a few different layers to this. The first and most obvious one is just the reliability problem. If you want ChatGPT or any chatbot to be the front end to the web, to be the thing I talk to instead of opening a browser and going to a bunch of different sites and apps, then it has to actually work most of the time. And with the current generation of models, when you ask them to do multi-step tasks, book a flight, compare prices, fill out a form, they fail at a pretty high rate. And the failures are not graceful. They don't say "I'm not sure." They confidently do the wrong thing. For an interface, that's kind of fatal, because the whole value proposition of delegating is that you don't have to check the work. If I have to verify every step, I might as well have done it myself.

The second layer, which I think gets less attention, is that this is fundamentally an adversarial setting, not a cooperative one. When you browse the web yourself, there's all kinds of content out there trying to manipulate you, ads, dark patterns, SEO spam, and you've developed a lot of intuition for filtering that. A language model acting on your behalf is reading all of that text as instructions, essentially. Prompt injection is the technical name, but the broader issue is that the model can't really distinguish between what you told it to do and what some webpage is telling it to do. That's not a bug you patch, it's pretty deep in how these systems work. So the more autonomy you give the agent, the bigger the attack surface.

And then the third layer is incentives, which is the one I find most interesting as someone who studies the tech industry and not just the technology. The web as it exists is built on a bargain where sites give you content and in exchange they get your attention, your data, the chance to show you ads or upsell you. If a chatbot sits between you and the site, that bargain breaks. The site doesn't get the eyeballs, it just gets a bot scraping the information and delivering a summary. So why would Expedia or a newspaper or a restaurant reservation system want to cooperate with that? Some of them are going to block it, some are going to negotiate for cuts of the revenue, some are going to try to manipulate the model's outputs the way they manipulate Google rankings today. The plugin and app store approach is an attempt to solve this with business deals rather than technology, but that just means you get a curated, gatekept version of the web rather than a universal one.

So when people say ChatGPT is going to be the new operating system or the new browser, I think they're underestimating all three of these. Not that it can't happen in some form, but the vision of a single conversational interface to everything runs into technical limits, security limits, and economic limits all at once, and the economic ones might be the hardest.

r001.rationale: It describes the chatbot as the front end while websites supply content for it to scrape and summarize, reducing sites to sources behind the interface.

r002.rationale: It mentions plugins and app stores as a business-deal approach, but does not clearly frame direct provider connections as an alternative to a general web-navigating agent.

r003.rationale: It says sites may block or resist cooperation, but does not connect that reluctance to limited uptake of GPT integrations.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between understanding what a user wants and reliably carrying it out. A language model can be very good at interpreting a request, but that doesn’t mean it can successfully navigate every website or operate every app. Interfaces change, instructions can be ambiguous, and even a small error can matter if you’re booking a flight or moving money.

There’s also a security problem. If the assistant is reading a website, it has to distinguish information on that page from instructions it should obey. A malicious page might try to redirect the assistant’s behavior. Once the assistant has access to your accounts and can act on your behalf, that becomes a much more consequential problem.

And then there’s the question of whether websites and apps want to participate. They have their own business models and reasons to control the interaction with users. So making ChatGPT a universal interface isn’t just a matter of improving the model. It requires reliable integrations, clear permissions, and ways for users to understand and control what’s being done on their behalf.

r001.rationale: The response discusses integrations and providers’ business interests, but does not say that websites and apps would be reduced to backend data or service providers.

r002.rationale: It mentions reliable integrations, but does not frame connecting providers directly to ChatGPT as an alternative to building a general web-navigating agent.

r003.rationale: It notes that providers may have reasons to control user interactions, but does not connect their unwillingness to integrate with ChatGPT to limited uptake of GPT integrations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a big gap between being able to talk about how to do something and being able to reliably do it on your behalf. If you ask a chatbot a question, you can read the answer and decide whether it makes sense. If you ask it to book a flight or change something in an app, it has to interpret your intent, navigate the interface, and take the right actions. A misunderstanding can have real consequences.

And a universal interface has to work across all these different websites and apps, each with its own conventions, permissions, and edge cases. When it encounters something unexpected, does it ask you for clarification? Does it guess? If you have to supervise every step, you lose a lot of the benefit of delegating the task.

There’s also a security problem. The system is reading content from websites while acting with your authority. It needs to distinguish information on a page from instructions it should follow. Otherwise, someone who controls that content could potentially redirect what the agent does.

So natural language can be a useful interface, but that doesn’t by itself solve the reliability, security, and user-control problems involved in taking actions.

r001.rationale: The response discusses varied websites and apps as interfaces the agent must navigate; it does not say they would be reduced to backend data or service providers.

r002.rationale: It describes an agent navigating websites, but does not present direct service-provider connections to ChatGPT as an alternative.

r003.rationale: It says nothing about providers’ willingness to integrate or the uptake of GPT integrations.
